content.summary_of_the_paper:
This paper investigates which planning in decision-time and background planning [1] is better. The contributions are to show it theoretically and empirically. 

To do this, they divide the cases into two categories; i) classical instantiations, where the value estimator and model could be represented as a table and are easy to be learned, and ii) modern instantiations, where the value estimator and model are represented through Neural Network. For classical instantiations, they show experimentally and theoretically that background planning is better than or equal to decision-time planning when the model is learned well. For modern instantiations, they hypothesize that background planning could suffer more from updating the value estimators because it learns only through simulated trajectories. In contrast, decision-time planning uses real experience and shows it through experiments.


[1] Sutton, Richard S., and Andrew G. Barto. Reinforcement learning: An introduction. MIT press, 2018.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength
- I think that many people working in the Reinforcement Learning area are curious about which planning is better, and they address this in this paper. It is a good try just itself.
- By dividing the cases as classical and modern instantiations, they can effectively deliver their finding (when modeling is easy, background planning is on par or better than decision-time planning).
- Generalization of the policy (zero-shot transfer) could be another interesting point when comparing two planning. The authors evaluate that too.

Weaknesses
- The paper format is different from the given style file. It looks critical.
- This paper is hard to follow, at least for me. I think the main idea is good, but the framing and contents of this paper maybe need to be revised (e.g., too many abbreviations are used).

    - The classical and modern instantiations must be introduced before directly using them in the abstract or introduction. Or Changing it could be another way, like a tabular environment and a more complex one that is hard to represent through a table.

    - In the introduction, I can't entirely agree below sentence. Can we say we already know the transition modeling for Go or Atari games? [2,3]

        - > DT planning algorithms [20; 21; 13; 14] under the assumption that the exact model of the environment is known and for domains that allow for certain computational budgets, such as board games

    - In background, you assumed the agent could access the function $\mathcal{S}_M \rightarrow \mathcal{S}_A$. Why did you think like this?
        - > However, in these cases, we assume that the agent has access to a deterministic function ρ : S M→ S A

    - In section 4, Partitioning of the Model Space is too wordy. Why must the general partition be introduced in the main paper? It is not used. Why is the last paragraph required (more policies could reduce the size of PCM and PRM)? I think the concepts of PCM, PRM, PNM, and PXM prove the relationship between decision time and background planning. You can skip this just by introducing the definitions shortly.

    - In section 4.1, what is the meaning of the learning process blue?
        - > More specifically, for DT planning we study a version of the OMCP algorithm of Tesauro & Galperin [21] in which a parametric model is learned from experience (see Alg. 1), and for B planning we study a simplified version of the Dyna-Q algorithm of Sutton [15; 16] in which planning is performed until convergence with every model in the model learning process blue (see Alg. 4).

    - In Propositions, why are the decision-time planning and background planning a rollout policy and certainty-equivalence policy, respectively? Couldn't the decision-time planning be more than one step of PI, like you mentioned in section 3?

    - In section 4.2, does a combined model mean the model includes a parametric and non-parametric model?

    - In section 4.2, why decision-time planning performs more than one-step PI for modern instantiation while it was one-step of PI for classical instantiation?

    - In the TL setting part of section 4.2, what are the first and second? They are not clearly introduced before discussing their characteristics. 
        - > We now consider two standard TL settings that are more challenging than the TL setting in Sec. 4.1. There is a distribution of training and test tasks, differing only in their observations. In the first one, the agent's transfer ability is measured by how fast it adapts to the test tasks after being trained on the training tasks

    - In the TL setting of section 4.2, why did you use those two settings only?

    - In the TL setting of section 4.2, what do you think about decision-time planning for the adaptation setting (the first one)? You only discussed background planning.

    - Using the task name in your code is not good (e.g., SG or SCS9N1). Please use a more meaningful name like SG -> classical instantiations or Empty 10x10 -> easy mode of modern instantiations.

    - Please use the full name before using abbreviations.

    - In section 5, I recommend changing the below sentence by mentioning MDP and POMDP settings.
        - > while O E= S Ein the SG environment, O E= ̸ S Ein the MG environments.

    - Why did you use the POMDP setting for MG?

    - What is state aggregation? You didn't discuss it before using it in section 5.1.

    - In PP experiments of section 5.1, why must the goal be changed? Couldn't it be possible to fix the goal?

    - In section 5.2, why didn't you use multiple unroll for background planning? A fair comparison must be the same as decision-time planning rollout steps.

    - In Figure 4, background planning only from simulated experience totally failed. Could you test an easier setting for background planning? From this result, we can see that model learning is failed.

    - In Figure 4 (g-j), what is the meaning of the numbers (e.g., 0.35 or 0.25)?

    - In Figure 4 (h-j), are the results for zero-shot transferring? Then why do the performances increase through more interactions? It means somethings are trained.

[2] David Silver, Thomas Hubert, Julian Schrittwieser, Ioannis Antonoglou, Matthew Lai, Arthur Guez, Marc Lanctot, Laurent Sifre, Dharshan Kumaran, Thore Graepel, et al. A general reinforcement learning algorithm that masters chess, shogi, and go through self-play. Science, 362(6419):1140–1144, 2018.
[3] Ye, Weirui, et al. "Mastering atari games with limited data." Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 34 (2021): 25476-25488.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The novelty of this paper is good enough, at least for me, but its clarity and quality are not good to be accepted, I think. Some notations are used before introducing. Some assumptions look not reasonable (e.g., the agent has access to a deterministic function). Some settings are used without discussing (decision-time planning single roll-out for classical instantiations while doing multiple roll-outs for modern instantiations) and unclear notations (e.g., environment names). It looks reproducible.
content.summary_of_the_review: As I commented above, I like what this paper investigates. However, at least for me, it is hard to be understood. Some settings are used without discussing why they are used, like multiple roll-outs for modern instantiations but single-step roll-outs for classical instantiations. In addition, some notations are hard to understand (e.g., environment names) and some parts hurt to understand the overall flow (e.g., the Partitioning of the Model Space in section 4).

content.confidence: 5: You are absolutely certain about your assessment. You are very familiar with the related work and checked the math/other details carefully.
content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper presents a theoretical study and empirical evaluation of comparative performance of decision time and background planning. 'Classical' and 'modern' (that is, involving neural networks) instantiations of the algorithms are considered.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths: the paper raises an interesting question of relative performance and role of background and decision time planning in various algorithmic instantiations.

Weaknesses: the algorithms selected for comparison are 1) too few for a balanced comparison 2) not representative of SOTA in classic planning. The theoretical analysis is both trivial and not rigorous. The empirical evaluation is insufficient.

Details about weaknesses:

2 algorithms of both 'classical' and 'modern' style are used for comparison. There is a discussion in the appendix why these algorithms are appropriate, but the discussion does not convince me. Experiments on more algorithms are needed to demonstrate that these two algorithms are indeed representative.

Research in classical planning didn't stop in the nineties. In particular there are MCTS family of classical planning algorithms. I do not see this family represented. There are optimal and suboptimal, online and offline planning algorithms introduced in the last 20 years which do not involve neural networks. 

The theoretical part of analysis argues that in table-based model specification, model learning will eventually converge to the actual model, while that will not happen with functional representation of the model. It is not clear from the paper why it is true, and my knowledge contradicts this statement --- even with functional representation an algorithm can converge to the actual model. 

The empirical evaluation is performed on just a couple of toy domains. Planning and RL algorithms are designed to work on a broad range of challenging tasks rather than to excel on small grids. Empirical evaluation on toy domains cannot be reliably used to confirm theoretical conjectures.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The paper is very hard to read due to excessive use of abbreviations. I suggest that the paper be rewritten without the use of non-conventional abbreviations. 

It does not appear to me that the results presented in the paper are easily reproducible from the description, and the code and data for the experiments are not provided.
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper raises an interesting question but fails to answer the question in convincingly.
content.correctness: 2: Several of the paper’s claims are incorrect or not well-supported.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 1: The contributions are neither significant nor novel.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper compares the performance between decision-time (DT) and background (B) planning algorithms by abstracting their decision making process in a policy improvement framework. Three different task settings are considered: 1) planning (P) 2) planning+learning (PL) 3) transfer learning (TL). Two different versions of model-based DT and B planning algorithms are considered: Classical Instantiation (CI) in which both the models and the value estimators are tabular, and Modern Instantiation (MI) in which both the models and value estimators are neural networks. Experimental results are provided to show that in contrast with CI versions, DT planning outperforms B planning with the MI versions in PL and TL settings in a simple gridworld (SG) environment and also environments from MiniGrid (MG).
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths: This paper provides intuitive explanations along with dynamic programming (policy improvement) based formalization of the observed performance differences between DT and B planning algorithms in grid world environments. 

Weaknesses:

(1) Sec 4.1, Page 5: “model learning process blue (see Alg. 4)” - This might be a typo. 

(2) In both Fig 3 and 4, some subfigures are missing their legends. It would be perhaps better to have a consistent system of labeling the plots in all subfigures in a figure.

(3) Page 9, second sentence from the top: “mitigated by decreasing the search budget” - should it be “.. increasing the search budget” according to the results?

(4) Page 14, last bullet in B: “now the agent only performs planning after every episode” - This does not seem to be the case from the provided pseudocode.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The dynamic programming based analysis of the DT and B planning algorithms in this paper is primarily focused on the tabular setting. Though the paper includes simple explanations for how the tabular analysis could extend to the MI settings, it does not provide a rigorous formalization of such reasoning. Experiments are performed on a simple grid and a minigrid environment, but does not consider other benchmark environments (eg. https://www.cs.toronto.edu/~tingwuwang/mbrl.html).
content.summary_of_the_review: I recommend rejection of the paper in its current form. The results are primarily limited to a grid world setting, supporting the analysis in the simple tabular case (CI) but lacks rigorous analysis of the MI versions of DT and B planning in MBRL.
content.correctness: 2: Several of the paper’s claims are incorrect or not well-supported.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.

content.confidence: 3: You are fairly confident in your assessment. It is possible that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work. Math/other details were not carefully checked.
content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper provides a comparison between decision-time planning and background planning in terms of determining the conditions under which they are most effective. They provide both a theoretical analysis of the methods and an empirical demonstration of the claims made through the theoretical analysis. They consider both classical tabular RL methods and more modern implementations that include parametric approximation mechanisms. They try to keep their analyses independent of specific techniques by leveraging a dynamic programming interpretation for each planning style. They look at three different settings including a pure planning setting, a planning and learning setting and transfer learning setting. The central theoretical tool they leverage for their analysis is a partitioning of potential space of models into various sets with differing relation to the true model.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
To be completely transparent, I had reviewed an earlier version of this paper in a different conference. It is unfortunate to see that many of the issues I had raised in that venue still remain, so many of my comments would be a repetition of points I had raised in the earlier review.


Strength:
The most important strength of the paper is the fact that it is trying to look at an often overlooked but nonetheless important problem. I also believe that a rigorous theoretical study of when these methods should be used, is a useful and valuable work.

Negative:
With that being said, I don’t really believe that the work in its current form is necessarily adding to our understanding of when these two methods should be used and I have reservations about the specific theoretical framework used to derive these conclusions.

Theoretical Result and Nature of these Planning Methods: All four of the propositions listed in the paper, leverages the fact that DT algorithm would result in suboptimal plan for the specified plan when compared to a B algorithm. However, as the authors themselves point out there are many DT instances where the algorithm could be run to completion. You could still satisfy the propositions by having a B algorithm that stops before convergence or by using an algorithm that simply returns random policy in place of the DT algorithm. To me the central characteristic that differentiates the two groups of algorithms is the fact that DT operates in test time. As such, TL and P&L are excellent examples of when DT could be potentially useful, however one could come to that conclusion without leveraging the intuition about DT resulting in suboptimal policy.

Partitioning of Model Space: Now one of the central theoretical mechanisms used in the analyses is the partitioning of the space into these various subsets. However, it is worth noting that in most cases these partitions would not cover the entire space of possible models. Also the paper presents no discussion on how the different methods would fare when the model belongs to a group outside the specific partitions discussed.

Significance of the Results: Finally, the conclusion section of this paper makes the claim that the objective of the paper is not to provide practical insights into selecting algorithms. If that is the case, how are the results from this paper meant to help the RL community?
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The paper is reasonably well written. However, it was surprising to see that the related work section was mostly relegated to a subsection within the introduction. In addition to various works done in the context of RL and MDPs, there also exists a rich set of literature on comparing decision-time (or online) planning with background (or offline) planning from the symbolic planning community ([1]). Also it’s a bit misleading to say that the work follows the analysis presented in [2] (I am assuming the authors meant [2] and not the monograph that is currently listed). While [2] does focus on a DT setting, the success of the method isn’t attributed to the fact that they use a DT algorithm, but focuses on the fact that bellman operators initialized with values close to the optimal value result in better convergence. In terms of reproducibility the authors do include considerable details about the methods they tested in the appendix section, however the actual code they used was not included as a supplementary file.

[1] Ghallab, Malik, Dana Nau, and Paolo Traverso. Automated planning and acting. Cambridge University Press, 2016.

[2] Bertsekas, Dimitri. "Lessons from alphazero for optimal, model predictive, and adaptive control." arXiv preprint arXiv:2108.10315 (2021).
content.summary_of_the_review: As discussed, while I think the paper tries to look at an interesting problem, the current analysis is not sufficient to provide any insights that were previously unknown.
content.correctness: 2: Several of the paper’s claims are incorrect or not well-supported.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
